t.2.71.1: Then, when the tenth day had passed, the king's son, having completed his purification, caused the śrāddha rites to be performed on the arrival of the twelfth day.
t.2.71.3: As the funeral rites for that king, his son gave to the brāhmaṇas female and male servants, carriages, and very large houses.
t.2.71.2: He gave the brāhmaṇas jewels, wealth and abundant food, a herd of goats, many of them white, and cows as well, by the hundreds.
t.2.71.4: Then, at the time of daybreak on the thirteenth day, the mighty-armed Bharata, overwhelmed with grief, lamented.
t.2.71.5: With his throat choked by sobs, he came for the rite of purification, and at the foot of his father's pyre, deeply grief-stricken, he spoke these words.
t.2.71.6: Father, now that my brother Rāghava, to whom I was entrusted by you, has gone forth to the forest, I have been abandoned by you in this empty desolation.
t.2.71.7: The son who was, as it were, the only refuge of that helpless woman has been banished to the forest; abandoning that mother Kausalyā, where have you gone, father, O king?
t.2.71.8: And seeing that circle of ground, reddened with ashes, where the bones had been burnt, the place where his father's body had been extinguished, he sank into despair, groaning aloud.
t.2.71.9: But he, on seeing this, weeping and wretched, fell upon the ground, like Śakra's machine-hoisted banner tumbling down even as it is being raised.
t.2.71.10: Then all his ministers rushed up to him, the one of pure vows, who lay fallen, just as the seers once hastened to Yayāti when he fell at the end of his time.
t.2.71.11: Śatrughna too, seeing Bharata overwhelmed with grief, fell senseless to the ground, remembering the protector of the earth.
t.2.71.12: Like one gone mad, bereft of his senses and deeply grieved, he lamented, recalling again and again, now one and now another, each of his father's excellent qualities.
t.2.71.13: The fierce, unfathomable ocean of grief, sprung from Mantharā, teeming with Kaikeyī as its crocodile and made of the granting of boons, drowned him.
t.2.71.14: Father, where have you gone, leaving behind Bharata, so tender and young, ever cherished by you, now lamenting?
t.2.71.16: Though it is the very time for splitting apart, the earth does not split asunder, bereft as it is of you, the king, the knower of dharma, the great-souled one.
t.2.71.15: Surely it is you who indulge all of us with our choice of foods and drinks, garments and ornaments; who will do that for us now?
t.2.71.17: Now that my father has gone to heaven and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest, what power have I to go on living? I shall enter the fire.
t.2.71.18: Bereft of my brother and my father, I will not enter Ayodhyā, now empty, though once protected by the Ikṣvākus; I will enter the forest of austerities.
t.2.71.19: Hearing the lamentation of those two and beholding that calamity, all the attendants became still more grievously afflicted.
t.2.71.20: Then both Śatrughna and Bharata, dejected and exhausted, writhed upon the ground like two bulls whose horns have been broken.
t.2.71.21: Then Vasiṣṭha, the composed and learned family priest of their father, raised Bharata up and spoke these words to him.
t.2.71.22: Three pairs of opposites hold sway over all beings without distinction; and since these cannot be avoided, you should not be like this.
t.2.71.23: And Sumantra too, knower of the truth, raised Śatrughna up and consoled him, and made him hear of the arising and passing away of all beings.
t.2.71.24: Those two glorious tigers among men, having risen, shine forth like two separate banners of Indra, weathered by rain and sun.
t.2.71.25: As the two sons, red-eyed and speaking piteously, kept wiping away their tears, the ministers urged them on to perform the remaining rites.
